t: Subarrays Distinct Element Sum of Squares I — Incremental Distinct Counting
o: We must sum the square of the number of distinct values over all O(n^2) subarrays. With n ≤ 100 even a cubic brute force passes, but the natural technique — fixing the left endpoint and extending the right endpoint while maintaining the distinct set incrementally — gives O(n^2) and generalizes to much larger n.
k: Extending a window by one element increases the distinct count by at most 1, so the count can be maintained incrementally instead of recomputed.
Summing squares needs only the current count, so no extra data structures beyond a set are required.

a.n: Approach 1: Recompute distinct count per subarray
a.i: Enumerate every (i, j) pair and count distinct values with a fresh set. Simple and clearly correct for n ≤ 100.
s: Triple loop: for each start i and end j, build a set from nums[i..j].
Add set.size() squared to the answer.
a.t: O(n^3) — each of O(n^2) subarrays costs O(n) to build a set; fine for n ≤ 100

a.i: Fix the left endpoint i and grow j, adding nums[j] to a persistent set. The distinct count changes by 0 or 1 per step, giving O(1) amortized work per subarray.
s: For each i, reset an empty set and count = 0.
For j from i to n-1: insert nums[j]; if it was new, count++.
Add count squared to the answer.
a.t: O(n^2) — each subarray extends the window in O(1) amortized time

w: Always present the incremental version; the brute force only exists as a sanity baseline. Watch overflow: the answer can reach ~(n^2/2)*(n^2) ≈ 2.5e7 for n=100, which fits int, but in generalized versions use 64-bit. Follow-up: the Hard version asks for the sum of squares of subarray distinct counts modulo 1e9+7 with n up to 1e5, requiring a segment tree with lazy propagation over 'contribution of each left endpoint'.
